title: Making Wait Times more productive
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino starts from watching her three-year-old pause over a letter in an alphabet book and asks what wait time after a classroom question is really for. She identifies three failure modes: too little, too much, and a length that suits the majority but strands a few students who were genuinely trying. Using a biology scenario about mitochondria in muscle cells, she shows how a student can say dunno during silent wait time and only succeed after hearing peers. Her fix is to structure the wait rather than lengthen it: students write down the key relevant facts, optionally turn and talk, then are cold called. The routine costs no extra time and directs attention to the retrieval and linking the question requires.
points: The problem with wait time is often what students do during it, not how long it lasts.
Having all students write key facts after a question directs their thinking to relevant prior knowledge at no extra time cost.
Turn and Talk after the written step, followed by Cold Call, lets students correct errors before answering publicly.
Modelling the routine for the first few lessons makes it an embedded classroom routine.
quotes: When we pose a question to a class, it is important to provide sufficient Wait Time so that each student has the chance to formulate their response. However, there are a few ways this can go wrong:
The problem is during the Wait Time, that student (and possibly others) were either not doing what was asked of them or were genuinely trying to work out the answer and couldn’t in the time given.
Some students may find it embarrassing to admit they actually tried to answer a question but could not.

I think the answer isn’t about providing more time, but about structuring the time given in the first place. I have tweaked my practice slightly to ensure those few students have every chance to succeed and I believe this has been of benefit to all students.

By instructing students to write down key facts, I am directing their attention to relevant information that can help them answer questions. As with any other classroom routine, I model this technique the first few times so students know exactly what they are expected to do.
In my experience, if given all the tools and facts to work an answer out, students are more likely to attempt the question and even be successful at it.
